passages.t: Absalom steals the hearts of Israel
passages.happening:
Absalom provides himself with a chariot and horses and fifty men to run ahead of him. He rises early and stands by the road to the city gate. Whenever anyone comes with a case for the king, Absalom asks where he is from, and then says, “Look, your claims are good and right, but the king has no deputy to hear you” (verse 3). And he adds, “If only someone would appoint me judge in the land, then everyone with a grievance or dispute could come to me, and I would give him justice” (verse 4).

When anyone comes to bow before him, Absalom takes his hand and kisses him. ‘In this way he stole the hearts of the men of Israel’ (verse 6).

After four years he asks the king's leave to go to Hebron to keep a vow he made to the LORD in Geshur. “Go in peace,” said the king (verse 9). From Hebron Absalom sends messengers through all the tribes: at the sound of the horn, they are to proclaim him king in Hebron. Two hundred men from Jerusalem go with him as guests, ‘and they went along innocently, for they knew nothing about the matter’ (verse 11). He sends for Ahithophel, David's adviser, and the conspiracy grows stronger (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 14 brought Absalom home without justice or repentance. Chapter 15 shows the result. This is the heart of Nathan's warning that God would raise up trouble against David from his own house.

The city gate was where the elders sat and cases were decided, so a man standing by the road to it met everyone with a grievance. His chariot, horses and runners were the display of a royal heir. Normally a commoner would bow to a prince, but Absalom takes their hands and kisses them, a gesture of equality that flatters. His words also suggest a real weakness in David's kingdom: ordinary Israelites found it hard to get their cases heard.

The Hebrew idiom to steal the heart can mean to deceive, and both senses fit. He won their affection by deceiving them about himself and about his father. The heart, in Hebrew, is the center of will and loyalty, and the contest that follows is a contest for Israel's heart.

The standard Hebrew of verse 7 says forty years, which cannot fit David's reign. Some Greek copies and the Syriac read four, and the BSB follows them. Hebron was a shrewd choice. It was the old capital of Judah, where David was first crowned and where Absalom was born, and some in Judah may have resented the move to Jerusalem. That David's own tribe joined the revolt shows how deep the discontent ran. Ahithophel was David's most respected adviser. He may have been Bathsheba's grandfather, which would give him a motive of his own, but the text never draws that connection.
passages.later:
Years later another son of David, Adonijah, put on the same display: ‘And he acquired chariots and horsemen and fifty men to run ahead of him’ (1 Kings 1:5).

A vow to worship if God brought one safely home was a familiar kind of promise. Jacob made one on his way out of the land: ‘so that I may return safely to my father’s house, then the LORD will be my God’ (Genesis 28:21). Absalom turns such a vow into a cover.
passages.hard:
Absalom used a vow to the LORD as cover for a revolt, and two hundred men went with him knowing nothing. What does the Bible make of a leader who wins people this way?

The chapter does not hide what Absalom is doing. He flatters, he promises justice no one else will give, and he dresses his plan in religious duty. The narrator's own note protects the men who went with him: they went innocently. Being taken in is not the same as being guilty. The text names the deceit as Absalom's.

If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault. Being taken in by someone who seemed godly is not a sign of weak faith. You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust. If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities. A pastor or counsellor outside that church may help you sort out what happened. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Absalom offered people what they wanted to hear. Ask how you tell the difference between real leadership and flattery. And ask whether there is a grievance in your own heart that someone could use to steal it.

passages.t: David flees, and a foreigner stays
passages.happening:
A messenger comes to David: “The hearts of the men of Israel are with Absalom” (verse 13). David says to his servants, “Arise and let us flee, or we will not escape from Absalom!” (verse 14). His household goes with him. He leaves ten concubines to take care of the palace.

At the last house he stops, and his servants march past him: the Cherethites and Pelethites, and six hundred men from Gath. David turns to their leader, Ittai the Gittite. Why should a foreigner and an exile, who arrived only yesterday, go wandering with a king who does not know where he is going? ‘Go back and take your brothers with you. May the LORD show you loving devotion and faithfulness’ (verse 20).

But Ittai answered the king, “As surely as the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king may be, whether it means life or death, there will your servant be!” (verse 21). So Ittai and his men and their little ones march on. ‘Everyone in the countryside was weeping loudly as all the people passed by. And as the king crossed the Kidron Valley, all the people also passed toward the way of the wilderness’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The chapter turns David back into what he was before he was king: a man on the run, dependent on the loyalty of friends and the mercy of God. He does not wait to be besieged. He leaves to spare the city.

The Cherethites, the Pelethites and the men of Gath were foreign soldiers loyal to David himself. Ittai's six hundred were Philistines from Gath. The most loyal man in the chapter is a foreigner and an exile.

David's parting prayer for Ittai uses the great covenant pair, loving devotion and faithfulness. Ittai answers with the very loyalty David wished for him. He will be with the king in life or in death.

The Kidron Valley lies just east of Jerusalem. Crossing it and climbing the Mount of Olives took David toward the wilderness and the fords of the Jordan.
passages.later:
Ittai's oath echoes Ruth's to Naomi, another foreigner's pledge of loyalty in life and death: “For wherever you go, I will go, and wherever you live, I will live” (Ruth 1:16).

Psalm 3 is headed for this day: ‘A Psalm of David, when he fled from his son Absalom’ (Psalm 3:1).
passages.asks: Ittai chose to stay with David whether it meant life or death. Ask who has stood with you when standing with you cost them something. And ask whom you are standing with now, when it might cost you.

passages.happening:
Zadok is there, and the Levites with him carrying the ark of the covenant of God. They set it down, and Abiathar offers sacrifices until all the people have passed out of the city.

Then the king said to Zadok, “Return the ark of God to the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, He will bring me back and let me see both it and His dwelling place again” (verse 25). And if not, ‘then here I am; let Him do to me whatever seems good to Him’ (verse 26).

He tells Zadok to go back in peace with his son Ahimaaz, and Abiathar with his son Jonathan, and he will wait at the fords of the wilderness for word from them. So Zadok and Abiathar take the ark back to Jerusalem and stay there (verses 27-29).
passages.hearers:
David will not use the ark as a charm to secure God's help. The elders of Israel once carried it into battle to force a victory, and lost it (1 Samuel 4). David sends it home and puts himself in God's hands. He trusts God's will rather than trying to control it through holy objects.

He calls Zadok a seer, because priests could ask God's guidance for the king. And he turns his loyal priests into a link with the city: their sons will carry him the news.

His words in verse 26 are the spiritual center of the chapter. He is going out partly because of his own sin, and he meets it not with excuses but with trust.
passages.later: A psalm headed for this flight says that distance from the ark is not distance from God: ‘To the LORD I cry aloud, and He answers me from His holy mountain’ (Psalm 3:4).
passages.asks: David refused to use the ark to force God's hand. Ask in what ways people try to use religious things to control God. And ask whether you could pray David's words, ‘let Him do to me whatever seems good to Him’, about the thing you fear most.

passages.t: Weeping up the Mount of Olives
passages.happening:
‘But David continued up the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went up. His head was covered, and he was walking barefoot. And all the people with him covered their heads and went up, weeping as they went’ (verse 30).

Someone tells David that Ahithophel is among the conspirators. So David pleaded, “O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness!” (verse 31).

At the summit, where he used to worship God, his friend Hushai the Archite meets him with his robe torn and dust on his head. David sends him back: if he pretends to serve Absalom, he can defeat Ahithophel's counsel, and he can send word through the priests and their sons (verses 32-36). ‘So David’s friend Hushai arrived in Jerusalem just as Absalom was entering the city’ (verse 37).
passages.hearers:
Covering the head, walking barefoot and weeping were signs of mourning. The king of Israel leaves his city as a mourner.

The news about Ahithophel is the worst news of the day. His counsel was held in extraordinary regard, and David knows what it will mean against him. His prayer is short and specific, and he at once takes a practical step. The answer seems to arrive at the summit, at the place of worship, in the person of Hushai.

The text calls Hushai David's friend. David turns him into a spy inside Absalom's court. Prayer and prudent action go together here. The whole story of the revolt now becomes a contest between two advisers, and behind them stands God's own purpose.
passages.later: Psalm 3, headed for this flight, answers the covered head: ‘But You, O LORD, are a shield around me, my glory, and the One who lifts my head’ (Psalm 3:3).
passages.asks: David prayed, and then he did the next wise thing. Ask whether you tend to pray and do nothing, or act and never pray. And ask what it would look like to do both in the trouble you face now.
